subjective.topic: Ideology of Pakistan and the Two-Nation Theory
subjective.question: On what is the ideology of Pakistan based? Explain briefly.
subjective.answer: The ideology of Pakistan is based on Islam and the Two-Nation Theory. It holds that the Muslims of the subcontinent are a separate nation on the basis of their religion, culture, civilisation, law and way of life, and therefore they are entitled to a separate homeland where they can order their lives according to the teachings of the Quran and Sunnah.

subjective.topic: Ideology of Pakistan and the Two-Nation Theory
subjective.question: What is the Two-Nation Theory? State its main points.
subjective.answer: The Two-Nation Theory states that the Muslims and the Hindus of British India were two separate nations, not two communities of one nation. Their religions, cultures, heroes, festivals, laws of inheritance and marriage, food and social customs were all different and even opposed to each other. They could not live together in one state after the British left, so the Muslims demanded a separate homeland — Pakistan. Quaid-e-Azam expressed it in 1940: the Muslims are a nation by any definition of a nation.

subjective.topic: Allama Iqbal — Life, Education and Role
subjective.question: From which university did Allama Iqbal earn his Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree?
subjective.answer: Allama Iqbal earned his B.A. from the University of Cambridge, England, where he studied at Trinity College. He had gone to England in 1905 for higher education; during the same stay he also qualified as a barrister from Lincoln's Inn, and in 1908 he received his PhD from the University of Munich, Germany.

subjective.topic: Allama Iqbal — Life, Education and Role
subjective.question: Give a brief account of the educational career of Allama Iqbal.
subjective.answer: Allama Iqbal received his early education at Sialkot. He passed his F.A. from Murray College, Sialkot, and then joined Government College, Lahore, from where he passed his M.A. in Philosophy in 1899 and was awarded a gold medal. In 1905 he went to England, took his B.A. from Trinity College, Cambridge, and qualified as a barrister from Lincoln's Inn. In 1908 he was awarded a PhD by the University of Munich for his thesis on the development of metaphysics in Persia.

subjective.topic: Allama Iqbal — Life, Education and Role
subjective.question: What did Allama Iqbal demand in his Allahabad Address of 1930?
subjective.answer: Presiding over the annual session of the All-India Muslim League at Allahabad in December 1930, Allama Iqbal demanded the creation of a separate Muslim state in North-West India. He proposed that Punjab, the North-West Frontier Province, Sindh and Baluchistan should be amalgamated into a single Muslim state. This address gave the Muslims a clear political goal and is regarded as the first formal demand for a separate Muslim homeland.

subjective.topic: Chaudhry Rehmat Ali and the Name Pakistan
subjective.question: When did Chaudhry Rehmat Ali become a clerk?
subjective.answer: Chaudhry Rehmat Ali became a clerk in 1918. After passing his B.A. from Islamia College, Lahore, in 1918, he took up a job as a clerk at Aitchison College, Lahore, where he later also served as tutor and house master, before leaving for England in 1930 for higher studies at Cambridge.

subjective.topic: Chaudhry Rehmat Ali and the Name Pakistan
subjective.question: Who coined the name "Pakistan"? Explain what the letters of the word stand for.
subjective.answer: The name "Pakistan" was coined by Chaudhry Rehmat Ali in his pamphlet "Now or Never" (1933). The word is made of letters taken from the names of the Muslim-majority regions of North-West India: P for Punjab, A for Afghania (the North-West Frontier Province), K for Kashmir, S for Sindh, and TAN for Baluchistan. The word also means "land of the pure" (Pak = pure, istan = land/place).

subjective.topic: Chaudhry Rehmat Ali and the Name Pakistan
subjective.question: Write a note on Chaudhry Rehmat Ali's pamphlet "Now or Never" (1933).
subjective.answer: On 28 January 1933, Chaudhry Rehmat Ali, then a student at Cambridge, issued a four-page pamphlet titled "Now or Never; Are We to Live or Perish For Ever?" In it he used the name "Pakistan" for the first time for the proposed separate Muslim homeland in North-West India and appealed to the British and Indian leaders to grant the Muslims their separate national existence instead of a place in an all-India federation. In the same year he founded the Pakistan National Movement in England to propagate this demand.

subjective.topic: Khilafat Movement and Its End
subjective.question: What were the main causes of the Khilafat Movement?
subjective.answer: The Khilafat Movement was launched by the Muslims of India in 1919 to save the Ottoman Caliphate (Khilafat) of Turkey, which the victorious Allied powers intended to abolish and dismember after the First World War. Its causes included the religious attachment of Indian Muslims to the Caliph as the head of Islam, the harsh peace terms being imposed on Turkey, the British failure to honour wartime promises about the safety of the Khilafat and the holy places, and the general anger caused by events such as the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919.

subjective.topic: Khilafat Movement and Its End
subjective.question: What happened after the abolition of the Khilafat?
subjective.answer: In March 1924, Mustafa Kemal Atatürk abolished the Caliphate in Turkey itself and sent the last Caliph, Abdul Majid II, into exile. With the very institution they were struggling to protect abolished by the Turks themselves, the Khilafat Movement in India lost its purpose and came to an end. The Khilafat Committee faded away, Hindu-Muslim unity built during the movement weakened, and Muslim leaders turned their attention to organising the Muslims of India politically, which strengthened the Muslim League in the following years.

subjective.topic: Khilafat Movement and Its End
subjective.question: Who abolished the Caliphate and when? Name the last Ottoman Caliph.
subjective.answer: The Caliphate was abolished by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder and first President of the Republic of Turkey, on 3 March 1924, when the Turkish Grand National Assembly passed the law ending the institution. The last Ottoman Caliph was Abdul Majid II, who was deposed and sent into exile immediately after the abolition.

subjective.topic: Non-Cooperation Movement and the Chauri Chaura Incident
subjective.question: What was the Chauri Chaura incident?
subjective.answer: The Chauri Chaura incident took place on 4 February 1922 at Chauri Chaura, a small town in the Gorakhpur district of the United Provinces. A procession of Non-Cooperation and Khilafat volunteers clashed with the police, who fired on the crowd. The enraged mob attacked the police station and set it on fire, killing 22 policemen who were trapped inside. This act of violence shocked Mahatma Gandhi and changed the course of the freedom movement.

subjective.topic: Non-Cooperation Movement and the Chauri Chaura Incident
subjective.question: Why did Mahatma Gandhi call off the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922?
subjective.answer: Gandhi called off the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922 because it had turned violent at Chauri Chaura, where a mob burnt a police station and killed 22 policemen. Gandhi believed in strictly non-violent (ahimsa) struggle and held that the people were not yet disciplined enough for a mass civil disobedience movement. He therefore suspended the movement, a decision that disappointed many leaders, and he was soon arrested and sentenced to six years' imprisonment.

subjective.topic: Second World War and the Pakistan Movement
subjective.question: When did the Second World War begin and end? Give the dates.
subjective.answer: The Second World War began on 1 September 1939, when Germany invaded Poland; Britain and France declared war on Germany two days later, on 3 September 1939, and the Viceroy declared India a party to the war without consulting the Indians. The war ended in 1945 — Germany surrendered in May 1945 and Japan formally surrendered on 2 September 1945.

subjective.topic: Second World War and the Pakistan Movement
subjective.question: Write a short note on the Cripps Mission (1942).
subjective.answer: The Cripps Mission was sent by the British Government to India in March 1942 under Sir Stafford Cripps, during the Second World War, to win Indian cooperation in the war effort. It offered India dominion status after the war and a constitution-making body, with a provision that any province could opt out of the future union. The Muslim League rejected it because the demand for Pakistan was not accepted clearly, and the Congress also rejected it, after which Gandhi launched the Quit India Movement in August 1942.

subjective.topic: Second World War and the Pakistan Movement
subjective.question: What was the Day of Deliverance (1939) and why was it celebrated?
subjective.answer: When the Second World War broke out in 1939, the Viceroy declared India at war without consulting the provincial governments, so the Congress ministries in the provinces resigned in protest. The Muslims had suffered under the Congress rule of 1937–39, so on Quaid-e-Azam's call the Muslim League celebrated 22 December 1939 as the Day of Deliverance (Youm-e-Nijat), thanking God for deliverance from Congress rule.

subjective.topic: Transfer of Power 1947 and the Governor-General Issue
subjective.question: Who wanted to become the Governor-General of both India and Pakistan in 1947? What was Quaid-e-Azam's response?
subjective.answer: Lord Mountbatten, the last Viceroy of India, wished to remain as the common Governor-General of both dominions, India and Pakistan, after independence. Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah firmly refused this proposal for Pakistan and decided to hold the office himself, so that the new state would be fully sovereign in practice as well as in name. Mountbatten therefore became Governor-General of India only, while Quaid-e-Azam became the first Governor-General of Pakistan.

subjective.topic: Transfer of Power 1947 and the Governor-General Issue
subjective.question: Write a short note on the 3rd June Plan (1947).
subjective.answer: The 3rd June Plan, also called the Mountbatten Plan, was announced by Lord Mountbatten on 3 June 1947. It laid down the partition of British India into two independent dominions, India and Pakistan. The assemblies of Punjab and Bengal were to vote on the partition of their provinces, referendums were to be held in the North-West Frontier Province and Sylhet, and power was to be transferred in August 1947. Both the Congress and the Muslim League accepted the plan, and it was implemented through the Indian Independence Act of July 1947.

subjective.topic: Transfer of Power 1947 and the Governor-General Issue
subjective.question: Who was the first Governor-General of Pakistan, and when did he assume office?
subjective.answer: Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah was the first Governor-General of Pakistan. He took the oath of office at Karachi in August 1947, at the birth of Pakistan on 14 August 1947, and held the office until his death on 11 September 1948. Lord Mountbatten, who had wanted to be Governor-General of both dominions, administered the transfer of power and himself became Governor-General of India.

subjective.topic: Transfer of Power 1947 and the Governor-General Issue
subjective.question: Why did Quaid-e-Azam refuse to accept Lord Mountbatten as the Governor-General of Pakistan?
subjective.answer: Quaid-e-Azam refused because accepting a common Governor-General would have compromised Pakistan's sovereignty and kept the new state under an authority also serving India. He also had serious differences with Mountbatten, whose impartiality he doubted after the handling of the partition and boundary questions. By taking the office himself, Quaid-e-Azam gave Pakistan a head of state who owed allegiance to Pakistan alone.
